concept.body: Arc measure is DEFINED as the central angle standing on it — a pure count of turning, independent of the circle's size. The whole circle is 360°, so arcs on the same circle add up: the major arc is 360° minus the minor. Minor arcs (<180°) take two-letter names; major arcs (>180°) take three.

explanationVariants: 360 − 100 = 260° — over 180, so it's the major arc.
Everything the minor arc didn't take: 260°.

widget.prompt: A minor arc measures 100°. The major arc between the same endpoints measures ?

commonErrors.feedback: 80 = 180 − 100 supplements on a straight line — circles supplement to 360: 260°.
100° repeats the minor arc — the major arc is the REST of the circle: 260°.

steps.body: Circles measure turning, and the ruler is the **central angle** — vertex at the center, sides on two radii. The piece of circle it cuts off is an **arc**, and we simply DEFINE the arc's measure to equal its central angle. A 140° central angle stands on a 140° arc; the whole circle is 360°.
The central angle IS the arc.

widget.prompt: Open the arc until the central angle reads 140°. Notice that the arc and the angle at the centre are the same number.
widget.successFeedback: 140° of arc, 140° at the centre. A central angle does not measure something *about* its arc — it IS its arc, in degrees.
widget.lowFeedback: The central angle is still under 140°. It always equals the arc, so widen the arc.
widget.highFeedback: Past 140°. The central angle equals the arc exactly, so pull the arc back.

predict.prompt: The arc starts at 80°. The CENTRAL angle that cuts it off measures…
predict.reveal: A central angle and its arc share one measure — the arc is simply the slice of circle the angle's arms cut off. Pin this baseline: the surprises start next lesson, when the vertex leaves the center and the angle drops to HALF.

cml.actionGoal: Move points on a circle while arc, central-angle, and inscribed-angle measures update together.

explanationVariants: The circle totals 360°: the major arc is 360 − 140 = 220°.

widget.prompt: A central angle of 140° marks off a minor arc of 140°. What is the measure of the MAJOR arc (the rest of the circle)?

commonErrors.feedback: 140° is the MINOR arc again — the major arc is everything else: 360 − 140 = 220°.
40 = 180 − 140 supplements as if arcs lived on a line — they live on a 360° circle: 220°.
110 = (360 − 140)/2 halves the leftover — the major arc takes ALL of it: 220°.

steps.body: Naming keeps the two arcs straight: **minor arcs** (under 180°) use two letters — arc AB — while **major arcs** (over 180°) borrow a third point to force the long way around — arc ACB. A 180° arc is a **semicircle**, cut off by a diameter. Adjacent arcs simply add, like segment lengths on a bent ruler.

explanationVariants: The three arcs tile the whole circle: 110 + 95 + x = 360, so x = 155°.
Subtract the known arcs from the full turn: 360 − 205 = 155°.

widget.prompt: Three points split a circle into arcs of 110°, 95°, and x. Find x.

commonErrors.feedback: 205 = 110 + 95 is the two KNOWN arcs combined — x is what remains: 360 − 205 = 155°.
77.5 halves the answer — x is one whole arc, not a split share: 155°.
25 treats the total as 230-ish — the full circle is 360°: 360 − 110 − 95 = 155°.

explanationVariants: 230° exceeds 180° — a major arc, which takes the three-letter name to force the long route.
Over half the circle: major, three letters.

widget.prompt: An arc measures 230°. How is it classified and named?

options.label: Major arc — three letters, like arc ACB
options.feedback: Past 180° the short two-letter name would point the wrong way; the middle letter pins the long route.

options.label: Minor arc — two letters
options.feedback: Minor arcs stay UNDER 180°. At 230° this is major, and needs the third letter.

options.label: Semicircle — either naming works
options.feedback: A semicircle is exactly 180°, the knife-edge case. 230° is past it: major arc.

options.label: It can't exist — arcs cap at 180°
options.feedback: Arcs run all the way to 360° — anything over 180° is simply major.

widget.prompt: A clock's minute hand sweeps from 12 to 7. Each hour-mark is one twelfth of the circle. What arc measure did it sweep?

commonErrors.feedback: 180° stops at 6 (half the circle). Seven of the twelve steps: 7 × 30 = 210°.
35 = 7 × 5 counts MINUTES-style — each hour step is 360/12 = 30 degrees: 210°.

hints: The arcs share 360° in the ratio 2 : 3 : 4 — nine equal parts in all.
explanationVariants: One part is 40°, so the arcs run 80°, 120°, 160° — and the largest is 160°.

widget.prompt: Three points cut a circle into arcs in the ratio 2 : 3 : 4. Find the LARGEST arc's measure.

commonErrors.feedback: 40° is ONE ratio part (360/9) — the largest arc claims four parts: 160°.
80° is the SMALLEST arc (2 parts). The largest takes 4: 160°.
180 = 4/8 of 360 misplaces the total parts — 2 + 3 + 4 = 9 parts, so 4 × 40 = 160°.

takeaways: Central angle = arc measure, by definition; the full circle is 360°.
Minor (<180°, two letters), major (>180°, three letters), semicircle (exactly 180°).
Adjacent arcs add; ratios split 360° into equal parts.
steps.teaser: Next: move the vertex from the center to the circle itself — and watch the angle halve.
